column2: “D-did I really get that fat?”
“That's not what I meant!{r}{p}...Although, well, you have put on weight, it's true.”
{n2} took off her goggles too and showed me a smile.
Seeing that smile for the first time in hours was like the sun peeking out from behind the clouds.
I looked at {n2} again.
Her long black hair stood out beautifully against the white ski wear.
Gliding down any tough slope with ease, she had been the center of attention on the slopes.
I think everyone must have expected a beautiful face beneath those goggles.
That's how ski resorts are.
With {n2}, I thought,
she surely wouldn't disappoint anyone.
I'd been fed up all afternoon with {n2}, a snow-country native, rubbing in the difference in our skills, but right now I felt proud.
I knew not only her face, but also how attractive the figure hidden under that thick ski wear was.
“One more run. Shall we?”
“Whaaat?{r}{p} You still want to ski?”
I asked back, worn out.
“Don't say that, come on.{r}{p} Just one more.{r}{p} Just one, okay?”
{n2} gave me her best smile and pressed her hands together.
I'm weak to that smile.
“Fine.{r}{p} But only one more.”
I agreed reluctantly.
Maybe I'd improved a little: I fell less and made it down before sunset.{g}
“All right, time to head back.”
I'd met {n2} this April at the university.
Through bold and persistent attacks, I'd managed to get as far as having dates with her, and that was this autumn.
No matter how hard I pushed there was never any response, and it even felt like I was wrestling alone, so honestly I was surprised when she was the one to invite me to go skiing together.
Her uncle and aunt run an inn in Shinano {C3}(now Nagano){C0}, she said.
It's a bit far from the ski resort and inconvenient, so even in season it apparently has few guests, and they'd let us stay for a bargain price.
Of course I gladly said yes, and yesterday, December 21st, we arrived here in Shinano.
By the time we got back to the inn in the 4WD borrowed from {n2}'s uncle, Jiro Kobayashi, it was completely dark and snow had started falling.
The Kobayashis' inn was called “Spur,” a name that seemed made to appeal to ski tourists.
With its log-cabin look, stylish white-based interior, and a wide variety of dishes, multinational or maybe stateless, all of them delicious, it was anything but deserted
: apparently magazines had even featured it and it was getting popular.
That “bargain price because it's slow” was something Mr. Kobayashi said so that {n2} and I wouldn't feel indebted; I realized that
after arriving.
Unfortunately, or rather naturally, {n2} and I had separate rooms.
We went back to our rooms to change, then met in the lounge beside the first-floor entrance.
On the sofas set around a large table, some guests were relaxing until dinner began.
“Well, well, you two lovebirds.{r}{p} Looks like you got your fill of skiing.”
Mr. Kayama said sarcastically when he saw my utterly exhausted face.
He's the president of a company in Osaka and apparently an old friend of Mr. Kobayashi.
A middle-aged man, with laugh lines and a shiny bald head that stood out.
Before I could reply, {n2} cut in.
“I wanted to ski a bit more, actually.”
She gave me a sidelong glance.
I shrugged, but said nothing in particular.
Beside Mr. Kayama sat his wife.
She looked no more than thirty-something, but I didn't know her real age.
Her name was Haruko.
And that Mrs. Haruko said to me with a coquettish laugh:
“These days it seems the girls have more energy, don't they?”
Exactly right.
I nodded inwardly, looking at the trio of office ladies who seemed to have arrived today.
“Oh, noooo!{r}{p} Kana, stop it!”
They had spread out what looked like a guidebook and were giggling, talking about something we couldn't hear.
The girl in the middle, thin with long hair, was marking the magazine with a red pen.
She was the one called Kana.
Was it a restaurant they had their eye on, or something?
The one on the right was called Keiko.
A cute, slightly plump girl with short hair.
The one on the left, with big glasses, seemed to be named Aki.
“Which one's your type?”
{n2} whispered in a cold voice.
“That's not it!{r}{p} I wasn't looking with that in mind...”
Just as I was about to make excuses, the cuckoo clock on the wall struck seven.
